Posted March 9, 2000
March 6, 2000
From The Eastern Daily Press
EDPLetters@ecn.co.uk
http://www.ecn.co.uk/
By Paul Hill

CUSTOMS NOT SOFT ON CANNABIS

Customs officials deny they will be " soft " on cannabis smugglers, despite a shift in national policy.

East Anglia's anti-drug smuggling teams have been told to dedicate more resources and intelligence work to Class A drugs, particularly heroin, even though cannabis accounts for the vast majority of drug seizures and possession cases.
(MarijuanaNews note: Perhaps it would be more accurate to say that they " have been told to dedicate more resources and intelligence work to Class A drugs, particularly heroin, BECAUSE cannabis accounts for the vast majority of drug seizures and possession cases. "

This is a case of more realistic policies conflicting with the same old prohibitionist dogma, and the economics of contraband. In reality, given that marijuana is far bulkier and easier to detect than most hard drugs, Customs will continue to find more cannabis.

Only the full legalization of cannabis will end this nonsense.)

Figures for 1998, published by the Home Office last month, showed that cannabis accounted for three-quarters of the 149,000 drug seizures.

The customs policy shift mirrors the approach of Whitehall's drugs " tsar " Keith Hellawell, who wants to concentrate on Class A drugs and the effect they have on other crimes.
See
As It Becomes Clear That He Has No Political Future, The UK Drugs Tsar Rediscovers His Conscience.

John Barber, spokesman for HM Customs and Excise in East Anglia, said that there was no question of being soft on cannabis.

Officers would still pursue cannabis cases if they found concealed consignments during checks at ports and airports.
See
UK " Gangbusters Are Warning The Government That Going Soft On Cannabis Laws Will Trigger A New Drugs Crisis. "

" But we have been asked to put more resources and intelligence effort into Class A drugs as theses are seen as being more dangerous ".

Mr Hellawell believes the use of soft drugs should remain a criminal offence, but thinks drugs should be targeted according to the " relative harm they cause. "
See
A Proposal For A Rational Allocation Of Drug Education Budgets
Based On The Harm Done By Various Substances -- Analysis By Richard Cowan

The customs policy change follows targets by the Government to halve the number of under 25's using heroin by 2008, and reduce the number of users by a quarter by 2005.
